nodes.summary: For a bit list $x$, the answer is the list $x$ with the bit $\mathrm{true}$ put in front if the cell-by-cell check of $x$ from the key $(0, 0)$ succeeds, and the one-bit list $[\mathrm{false}]$ otherwise.

nodes.summary: For a bit list $x$, the list of natural numbers $l$ whose cells are $x$, if there is one, and nothing otherwise. Here the cells of $l$ are its numbers written in order, each number $n$ as $n$ copies of $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one $\mathrm{false}$; distinct lists have distinct cells. The decoder reads one cell at a time with the unary length reader.

nodes.summary: For every bit list $x$, the cell-by-cell check of $x$ from the key $(0, 0)$ succeeds if and only if the decoding of $x$ as a code stack returns a code.
nodes.title: The cell-by-cell check agrees with code-stack decoding

nodes.summary: The check of a bit list $x$ from a key $(p_q, p_a)$ of natural numbers is defined as follows. The empty list passes. Otherwise, calling the cell of a number $n$ the $n$ bits $\mathrm{true}$ followed by one bit $\mathrm{false}$, read four cells off the front of $x$, those of $q$, $a$, $q'$ and $s$ in this order, leaving the rest $r$. The check fails if one of these cells cannot be read because what remains contains…
nodes.title: Cell-by-cell check of a code stack

nodes.summary: For every bit list $x$ and every code $c$, if $x$ decodes to $c$, then the code stack of $c$ is $x$.
nodes.title: Decoding inverts the code stack

nodes.summary: Let $E$ be a list of entries $(q, a, q', s)$ of natural numbers, and let $Q$ and $M$ be the sums, over the entries of $E$ counted with multiplicity, of $q + 1$ and of $a + 1$ respectively. The code of $E$ has a table with $Q$ rows and $M$ columns, and for $q < Q$ and $a < M$ its position $(q, a)$ holds $(q', s)$ for the first entry $(q, a, q', s)$ of $E$ with key $(q, a)$, and is empty (halting) if $E$ has no entry…

nodes.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $f(0) = 0$. Then no decision problem is decided by a code within $f(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$: the time class $\mathrm{CodeTime}(f)$ is empty. With no step on the empty input, the tape stays blank and holds no answer bit.
nodes.title: Some step is needed

nodes.summary: Let $t, t' : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $t(n) \le t'(n)$ for every $n$. Then every decision problem that some code decides within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$ is decided by some code within $t'(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$: $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t) \subseteq \mathrm{CodeTime}(t')$.
nodes.title: Monotonicity of time classes on codes

nodes.summary: Let $f, g : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ with $f(n) \le g(n)$ for every $n$, and for a time bound $t$ let $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t)$ be the class of decision problems that some code decides within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$. If the diagonal language $\mathrm{diag}(f)$ belongs to $\mathrm{CodeTime}(g)$, then $\mathrm{CodeTime}(f)$ is a proper subclass of $\mathrm{CodeTime}(g)$.
nodes.title: A hierarchy within codes, given an upper bound

nodes.summary: For $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, $\mathrm{CodeTime}(t)$ is the class of decision problems $L$ such that some code decides $L$ within $t(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$.
nodes.title: Time classes on codes

nodes.summary: The component machine with the twelve stacks $X, Z, P, P_2, U, N, A_2, B_2, D, C, T, O$ of the layout machine, each holding bits, with the labels and the program of the layout machine, and with its stacks listed in the order $X, Z, P, P_2, U, N, A_2, B_2, D, C, T, O$.
nodes.title: The layout machine as a host component

nodes.summary: The component machine whose stacks are the input $X$ and the output $O$, each over the alphabet of bits, whose labels and program are those of the readout machine, which checks whether $X$ holds exactly $(\mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{true}, \mathrm{false})$ and pushes $\mathrm{false}$ on $O$ if so and $\mathrm{true}$ otherwise, and whose list of stacks is $(X, O)$.
nodes.title: The readout machine as a host component

nodes.summary: The component machine with the twelve stacks $X, Y, W, V, Q, A, P_Q, P_A, T_1, T_2, J, O$ of the checking machine, each holding bits, with the labels and the program of the checking machine, and with its stacks listed in the order $X, Y, W, V, Q, A, P_Q, P_A, T_1, T_2, J, O$.
nodes.title: The checking machine as a host component

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be the code whose table has one row, for state $0$: on the input symbols $1$ and $2$ it moves right and stays in state $0$, and on the blank $0$ it writes $1$, the symbol of the bit $\mathrm{false}$, and enters state $1$, which has no row, so that $c$ halts. Then $c$ decides the empty language within $n + 1$ steps on every input of length $n$.
nodes.title: The constant-false code decides the empty language

nodes.summary: Let $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ satisfy $n + 1 \le f(n)$ for every $n$. Then the empty language, the decision problem that answers false on every bit list, belongs to the time class of $f$: some code decides it within $f(|x|)$ steps on every input $x$, where $|x|$ is the length of $x$.
nodes.title: Time classes are not empty once the bound exceeds the input length

nodes.summary: The code whose table has a single row, for state $0$: on the blank $0$ it writes the symbol $1$, the symbol of the bit false, and enters state $1$; on the input symbols $1$ and $2$ it moves right and stays in state $0$; on every other symbol it halts. State $1$ has no row, so the machine halts there. This code answers false on every input.
nodes.title: The constant-false code

nodes.summary: A code $c$ decides a decision problem $L$ within the time bound $t : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ when, on every bit list $x$, the machine of $c$ started on the input word of $x$ halts within $t(|x|)$ steps, and its tape from the head rightwards, without trailing blanks, is the single symbol of the answer $L(x)$: $2$ for true and $1$ for false.
nodes.title: Deciding within a time bound

nodes.summary: For every code $c$, decoding the code stack of $c$ succeeds and returns a code $c'$ whose code stack equals the code stack of $c$.
nodes.title: Code stacks decode to codes with the same code stack

nodes.summary: For a bit list $x$, the decoding of $x$ as a code is defined as follows. Write the cell of a number $n$ for the $n$ bits true followed by one bit false, and the cells of a list of numbers for the cells of its numbers in order. If $x$ is the cells of a list $l$ of natural numbers (such an $l$ is unique), the length of $l$ is a multiple of $4$, and the keys $(q, a)$ of the entries $(q, a, q', s)$ formed by the…
nodes.title: Decoding a code stack

nodes.summary: For every clocked result $o$, either a timeout or the output of a halted run, the diagonal answer of $o$ is true exactly when the output encoding of $o$ differs from the output encoding of the result whose output is the single symbol $2$ of the bit true, which is the bit list true, true, true, false.
nodes.title: The diagonal answer read from the encoded output

nodes.summary: For a clocked result $o$, either a timeout or the output of a halted run, the diagonal answer of $o$ is false if $o$ is the output consisting of the single symbol $2$, the symbol of the bit true, and true otherwise, including on a timeout.
nodes.title: The diagonal answer

nodes.summary: For a time bound $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and a bit list $x$, the argument is a triple of a code, an input and a clock. If $x$ decodes to a code $c$, it is $(c, x, f(|x|))$. Otherwise it is the code with the empty table, the input consisting of the single bit true, and the clock $0$; that code halts at once with the answer true, so that the diagonal answer is false there.
nodes.title: The universal machine's argument for the diagonal language

nodes.summary: For every time bound $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every code $c$ with code stack $x$, the bit list $x$ belongs to the diagonal language for $f$ iff the output encoding of the result of running $c$ on $x$ for at most $f(|x|)$ steps differs from the output encoding of the result whose output is the single symbol $2$ of the bit true.
nodes.title: The diagonal language through the universal machine

nodes.summary: For every time bound $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every code $c$ with code stack $x$, the bit list $x$ belongs to the diagonal language for $f$ iff it is not the case that $c$, run on $x$, halts within $f(|x|)$ steps with output the single symbol $2$ of the bit true.
nodes.title: The diagonal language on a code stack

nodes.summary: For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every bit list $x$, let $(c, y, T)$ be the universal machine's argument for the diagonal language of $f$ on $x$. Then the diagonal language of $f$ holds at $x$ iff the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $y$ for at most $T$ steps, does not return the output $[2]$, the symbol of the answer true.
nodes.title: The diagonal language through the clocked evaluator

nodes.summary: For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ and every bit list $x$ that is the code stack of no code, $x$ is not in the diagonal language of $f$.
nodes.title: Bit lists that encode no code are outside the diagonal language

nodes.summary: For every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the diagonal language of $f$ is not in the time class of $f$ on codes: no code decides it on every input $x$ within $f(|x|)$ steps. This is the argument from the proof of Sipser's Theorem 9.10: a code $c$ deciding it would, on its own code stack, answer the opposite of the diagonal language of $f$.
nodes.title: The diagonal argument

nodes.summary: The diagonal language for the time bound $f(n) = n^2 + 1$, the set of bit lists $x$ that encode a code which does not halt on $x$ within $|x|^2 + 1$ steps with the answer $\mathrm{true}$, is in the class P of decision problems decidable in polynomial time.
nodes.title: The quadratic diagonal language is in P

nodes.summary: For $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$, the diagonal language of $f$ holds at a bit list $x$ iff $x$ encodes a code $c$ and the clocked evaluator, running $c$ on $x$ for at most $f(|x|)$ steps, does not return the output $[2]$, the symbol of the answer true: either $c$ does not halt on $x$ within $f(|x|)$ steps, or it halts with another output. Bit lists that encode no code are not in the language. This is the…

nodes.title: The reformatting function in bits

nodes.summary: A list of natural numbers is read as a list of entries $(q, a, q', s)$, four consecutive numbers per entry, if possible: the empty list gives no entries; a list that starts with $q, a, q', s$ and continues with $l$ gives the entry $(q, a, q', s)$ followed by the entries read from $l$, if that succeeds; and the reading fails when the length of the list is not a multiple of $4$.

nodes.summary: For a bit $b$ and a label $\ell$, the statement that pops the top of the input stack $X$ and goes to $\ell$ if the popped symbol is $b$, and to the label miss otherwise, including when $X$ is empty.

nodes.summary: A bit list $x$ encodes a code (its decoding succeeds) iff there is a list of entries $(q, a, q', s)$ of natural numbers whose keys $(q, a)$ strictly increase in lexicographic order, such that $x$ is the list of cells of the numbers of these entries, four numbers per entry.

Theory of Computation

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
